claims.claim: Birth, in developmental terms, is the process by which a baby moves from the womb into the world; the underlying account of childbirth as the baby's passage through the birth canal comes from OpenStax Lifespan Development.
The process of giving birth has three stages: labor (dilation), delivery, and afterbirth.
The first stage, labor, is marked by contractions that open and thin the cervix and is typically the longest stage, lasting several hours or more.
The third stage, afterbirth, is the expulsion of the placenta, which usually takes five to thirty minutes.

Newborns have reflexes — automatic, unlearned reactions such as rooting, sucking, grasping, and startle — and the presence and strength of reflexes is an important sign of nervous system development; many infant reflexes disappear as the child grows.
Newborns can hear, touch, taste, and smell, but vision is the least developed sense: they cannot see well or in color at first, and coordinated focusing develops over the first one to two months.
Newborn appearance varies; most weigh somewhere between about 5.5 and 10 pounds, and below about 5 lb 8 oz is considered low birth weight.
The Apgar test was introduced by Virginia Apgar, MD (1909-1974) in 1952 and is performed at one and five minutes after birth.

The Apgar scores five things — breathing effort, heart rate, muscle tone, reflex response, and skin color — each scored 0, 1, or 2; scores of 7-9 are normal, and a score of 10 is very unusual because nearly all newborns lose a point for briefly blue hands and feet.

Bonding — the caregiver's emotional connection to the newborn — can begin within minutes of birth and is distinct from attachment, the child's emotional connection to the caregiver, which develops over time.

Birth practices vary by culture and time: about 98 percent of US births occur in hospitals and about 1 percent at home, while globally nearly half of all births occur at home; birthing positions also vary, such as hands-and-knees in Nepal.
WHO lists essential newborn care for all babies, including thermal protection such as skin-to-skin contact between mother and infant and early breastfeeding.
The first month of life is the most vulnerable period for child survival, and quality care at and immediately after birth is central to newborn survival.
Oxytocin plays a role both in initiating labor and in forming bonds with others.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Numbering and naming of the stages of birth
positions: OpenStax Lifespan Development names the three stages as dilation, active labor, and afterbirth delivery.
Some clinical texts number the stages of labor differently, treating delivery itself as a numbered stage of labor.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows the developmental-text naming the task specifies — labor, delivery, afterbirth — and describes each in one factual line without clinical stage-numbering, which belongs to the nursing subject's obstetrics content.

positions: A score of 10 is often assumed to be the expected or perfect result.
MedlinePlus states that a score of 10 is very unusual because almost all newborns lose a point for blue hands and feet, which is normal right after birth; scores of 7-9 are normal.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches 7-9 as the normal range, 10 as rare, and stresses that the Apgar is a snapshot of the first minutes, not a prediction of later development.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is bonding a make-or-break first-minutes event?
positions: Early popular accounts suggested immediate contact at birth was critical for bonding.
OpenStax Lifespan Development states bonding can begin within minutes of birth but also develops over the first months, and that bonding may not happen immediately for everyone — that is okay.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents bonding as beginning at first contact but building over time, and flags attachment (the baby's side of the relationship) as the sibling topic that owns that deeper process.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft contained no verifiable factual claims; it described birth only as 'a foundational concept in Human Development' with generic study advice.
The draft's claim that birth is 'a concept students use to organize information, ask better questions, and explain relationships' is generic boilerplate, not a developmental claim about birth.

rightsIssues: OpenStax Lifespan Development pages carry a notice that the book may not be ingested into LLMs without permission; the pages are therefore recorded as REFERENCE_ONLY with aiIngestionAllowed false, and all facts were synthesized into original prose without reproducing source wording.

sourceRecords.title: OpenStax Lifespan Development, Section 2.4: Childbirth and Perinatal Health
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A open textbook. Canonical openstax.org URL registered; openstax.org blocks direct fetch, so the page was read via Internet Archive snapshot 20250108184803. Supports: the three-stage account of birth (dilation/labor, active labor/delivery, afterbirth delivery with the placenta expelled in about 5-30 minutes); labor as typically the longest stage (several hours, up to about twenty); the Apgar test as the first newborn test (five aspects, scoring 0-2 each); about 98% of US births in hospitals, about 1% at home, and nearly half of all births globally at home; birthing positions varying worldwide (hands-and-knees in Nepal; traditional upright in parts of Tanzania giving way to supine); obstetricians, midwives, and doulas as birth attendants; placenta customs varying by culture (buried, consumed, or made into memorabilia in some cultures); low birth weight below about 5 lb 8 oz and high weight about 9-10 lb; oxytocin's roles in initiating labor and forming bonds. Facts synthesized in original prose; no source wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: OpenStax Lifespan Development, Section 2.5: The Newborn in Context
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A open textbook. Read via Internet Archive capture (web.archive.org/web/2024/ of the canonical URL). Supports: bonding as the caregiver's one-way emotional connection that can begin within minutes of birth, motivated by oxytocin, and distinct from attachment, which develops over time; the newborn senses — hearing, touch, taste, and smell work while vision does not (no clear vision or color at first, focusing develops over one to two months); bonding is not lost if immediate contact is missed, and caregivers who miss it still have the first months to build a strong bond. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Apgar score (MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. National Library of Medicine, MedlinePlus
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports: the Apgar as a quick test at 1 and 5 minutes after birth; Virginia Apgar, MD (1909-1974) introduced the score in 1952; the five scored categories (breathing effort, heart rate, muscle tone, reflex irritability/grimace, skin color), each scored 0, 1, or 2; total scores of 7-9 as normal; a score of 10 as very unusual because almost all newborns lose a point for blue hands and feet, which is normal after birth; scores below 7 as a sign the baby needs medical attention. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Infant reflexes (MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. National Library of Medicine, MedlinePlus
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports: reflexes as automatic muscle reactions that happen in response to stimulation; the presence and strength of reflexes as an important sign of nervous system development and function; infant reflexes including rooting (turning toward a cheek touch and making sucking motions), sucking, grasp, Moro/startle, and step; many infant reflexes disappear as the child grows older. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
